statements.quote: The best of newsletter coverage of your wedding is in the future. Subscribe, and the above absurdist reporting about causal inference in statistics could be celebrating your nuptials too!
statements.context: Closing promotional line of a satirical correction post: the author admits the joyful 'family gathering' he reported on was a psychiatrist's wedding. He jokes that future paid subscribers could get absurdist newsletter coverage of their own weddings.
statements.note: Joke subscription pitch; no real expectation. Logged for recall only. Own newsletter; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Somebody, anybody, buy that company. And then offer a business associate agreement. Comply with HIPAA. Boom, you have a patient self-scheduling tool! Hospitals will pay a bazillion dollars for that.
statements.context: First item of a list of proposed health-tech companies in a post the author labels 'pure clickbait' and 'Only satire'. Conditional: if someone buys Calendly (not HIPAA compliant) and offers a business associate agreement, hospitals will pay a very large amount for a compliant patient self-scheduling tool. A footnote adds that Epic integration would make everybody more money.
statements.note: Author labels the post satire/clickbait; 'a bazillion dollars' is hyperbole. Conditional on an acquisition plus a BAA. The market thesis (compliant is the new disruptive) reads sincere.

statements.quote: Please buy Zapier. Somebody. Anybody. Sell the same product, but allow a business associate agreement to be signed. Now you can automate the internal workings of a healthcare business! Amazing. Billions. Overnight success!
statements.context: Second item of the satirical list. Conditional: if someone buys Zapier (which will not sign a business associate agreement) and allows a BAA, the same product becomes a healthcare automation business worth billions and an overnight success.
statements.note: Author-labelled satire; 'Billions. Overnight success!' is hyperbole. Conditional on an acquisition plus a BAA. Underlying thesis reads sincere.

statements.quote: It works because it's compliant, so these legacy technologies stay around like a cockroach after nuclear Armageddon.
statements.context: Opening argument (outside the satire list): fax machines and pagers persist in healthcare because communication over phone lines is exempt from additional HIPAA regulation. The author asserts these legacy technologies keep surviving; 'Fax machines do that to this day.'
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense description with an implied forecast that fax machines and pagers persist in healthcare.

statements.quote: Yeah, insurance won’t cover revolutionary treatments. However, the NTAP changes that if we leave comments.
statements.context: Call-to-action post on the CMS FY2024 inpatient prospective payment proposed rule (federalregister.gov 2023-07389) open comment period, with about nine days left. The author says insurance does not cover revolutionary depression treatment (SAINT neuromodulation) and that the New Technology Add-On Payment program changes that if readers leave comments.
statements.confidence_phrase: changes that if we leave comments
statements.note: Compound: current non-coverage plus a conditional claim that NTAP (with public comments) changes coverage.

statements.quote: It is not an overstatement to say that the capacity of SAINT Neuromodulation to achieve depression remission without the use of medications could revolutionize our approach to mental health treatment.
statements.context: From a sample CMS comment letter (Re: SAINT Neuromodulation NTAP Coverage) the author generated with GPT-4 and posted as a template for readers to adapt. The letter also calls the decision 'a watershed moment in the future of mental health care' and says SAINT 'could be a much-needed lifeline' for treatment-resistant patients.
statements.note: GPT-4-drafted sample letter; author calls it a parody of self-praise but endorses SAINT. Coder should weigh authorship.

statements.quote: NTAP coverage of SAINT Neuromodulation could help democratize access to this promising therapy, thereby improving the quality of life for countless individuals suffering from depression.
statements.context: Same GPT-4-drafted sample comment letter to CMS. Conditional: if CMS grants New Technology Add-On Payment coverage for SAINT, access to the therapy widens.
statements.note: GPT-4-drafted sample letter posted as a template; hedged conditional. Coder should weigh authorship.

statements.quote: I think it's cute they didn't just immediately make that above workplace a hospital. But it's obviously going to be a hospital. Just make a little adjustment, in the surgical OR, without having to touch anything!
statements.context: Satirical open letter written in Apple's voice after the Vision Pro announcement (June 5, 2023). Here the author's own voice breaks through: the workplace demo Apple showed will become a hospital use case, for example hands-free adjustments in a surgical operating room.
statements.note: Inside a satirical letter but reads as a sincere prediction of Vision Pro adoption in hospitals and operating rooms.

statements.quote: All your market share...are belong to us.
statements.context: Subtitle of the satirical open letter 'from Apple' to every other company after the Vision Pro reveal, claiming Apple takes everyone's market share; the letter closes 'It's been a pleasure pretending there are any other companies.'
statements.note: Meme joke ('All your base are belong to us'); satirical hyperbole about Apple dominance. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: CMS, aka the government, has proposed CHANGES to the rules that would allow Medicare to pay for New Technologies for Psychiatric Treatment (via the NTAP Program).
statements.context: Post urging readers to comment in the last days of the CMS proposed rule open comment period (federalregister.gov 2023-07389). Describes the proposal's effect: if adopted, Medicare would pay for new psychiatric technologies (SAINT is the only psychiatric treatment on the docket) in psychiatric hospitals via NTAP.
statements.note: Borderline: description of a proposed rule's effect, conditional on adoption.

statements.quote: We finally get a say on what the most major payer—medicare—does. This sets a precedent.
statements.context: The author claims the CMS decision on NTAP payment for a psychiatric treatment (SAINT) in psychiatric hospitals sets a precedent for how Medicare, the largest payer, pays for new psychiatric technologies.
statements.note: Implied forecast: this NTAP decision will shape later payer decisions on new psychiatric treatments.

statements.quote: Psychedelics? They will need this payment model.
statements.context: After saying the CMS NTAP decision sets a precedent, the author predicts psychedelic treatments will need an NTAP-style Medicare payment model to reach patients.
statements.note: Paired with the same claim for medical devices in the next line.

statements.quote: Medical devices? Of all kinds! They will need this payment model.
statements.context: Same passage: medical devices of all kinds will need an NTAP-style Medicare payment model, so the SAINT NTAP decision matters beyond SAINT.
statements.note: Paired with the psychedelics claim in the prior line.

statements.quote: In the near future one could, under Medicare, go to a hospital with depression and leave no longer depressed. 79% of the time.
statements.context: Describes SAINT as a technology that treats depression to remission in 5 days with no oral medication. If the NTAP proposal is adopted, Medicare patients could soon be treated to remission in a psychiatric hospital; 79% is the SAINT trial remission rate restated as a future expectation.
statements.note: Conditional on the NTAP proposal; compound (Medicare access plus a 79% remission rate).
